TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES (“ALJs”):
        By this Reply Brief, the Segment K13/K51 Landowners address only the arguments raised
against Routes CCG and 572 without repeating the evidence already set forth in support of Routes
CCG and 572.

   I.    Cost and habitable structure counts, by themselves, do not justify selecting Route
                                     894 over Routes CCG or 572.
        Several parties argue that Routes CCG and 572 should be rejected in favor of Route 894
because Routes CCG and 572 are more expensive and impact more habitable structures. That
argument treats cost and habitable structure counts as controlling, downplays the other statutory
and Commission rule criteria, and ignores the unique record in this case. A similar argument was
rejected in Docket No. 38290.
        G6 Landowners Legal Fund and Newman Group both give lip service to the requirement
that all of the statutory factors must be weighed, but then immediately pivot to stating that cost
and habitable structures alone justify eliminating CCG. G6 Landowners Legal Fund argues that
two “characteristics alone,” greater cost and habitable structures, justify eliminating Route CCG


                                                2
 (and presumably 572) from consideration as a best meets route compared to Route 894.1 Newman
Group argues that because length, cost, and habitable structures are primary strengths of Route
894 and the factors the Commission has treated as most important, “this record finding alone
provides a strong and independent basis for selecting Route 894.”2 Those arguments ultimately
reduce the routing analysis to the very kind of numerical exercise the Commission’s rules and case
law do not permit.
        The ALJs and Commission should reject that approach. No single factor is dispositive. The
Commission must weigh all statutory and regulatory criteria, and the weight assigned to a
particular criterion depends on the facts and circumstances of the case. Indeed, the Applicants
themselves correctly point out that the weight the Commission assigns to particular routing factors
may vary from case to case depending on the specific facts and circumstances. 3 That is critical
here. This docket involves the largest transmission facilities ever proposed in Texas, two important
state parks, significant viewshed evidence, two major Hill Country rivers, ESSS and critical-
habitat concerns, and historic ranchlands. Cost and habitable structures are important, but they are
not trump cards.
        The Route 894 proponents also fail to distinguish Docket No. 38290. In that case, the
Commission approved a route that was longer, more expensive, and impacted more habitable
structures in order to avoid the unique impacts associated with Palo Duro Canyon and Palo Duro
Canyon State Park.4 That precedent matters because it confirms that cost and habitable structure
counts, while important, do not automatically control where the record presents unique scenic,
recreational, environmental, community value, and engineering concerns.5 The same principle
applies here. Like Palo Duro Canyon State Park, this docket involves extraordinary public
resources and unique routing impacts to Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park
that should not be ignored in favor of a simple cost and habitable structure comparison.
        Docket No. 38290 is especially instructive because the route impacts there were not limited
to direct encroachment on a state park. The Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) recognized that Palo
Duro Canyon is “an iconic feature of the Texas landscape” and rejected Central-South routes even

 though those routes did not directly encroach on Palo Duro Canyon State Park.6 The problem was
broader: “these lines would likely be visible from portions of the state park.”7 The PFD focused
on actual viewshed and aesthetic impacts, not merely on whether the line crossed park property or
fell within a fixed distance from a park boundary. Indeed, although there were no parks or
recreational areas within 1,000 feet, the PFD still gave substantial weight to the evidence that links
on the Central-South corridor routes would be visible from portions of Palo Duro Canyon State
Park, including views from locations several miles away and even “well over 10 miles” away.8
        That reasoning applies with equal force here. Route 894 proponents ask the ALJs and
Commission to treat the EA’s one-half-mile FGVZ metric as if it were a hard cutoff for state park
impacts. But Docket No. 38290 shows that the Commission is not limited to rigid proximity
metrics when evaluating scenic, recreational, and community value impacts to iconic public
resources. In that docket, the Commission considered viewshed impacts even where the
transmission line was outside a 1,000-foot metric and visible from much greater distances.9 Here,
Link J22 comes within 0.61 miles of Post Oak Ridge State Park, and the record includes substantial
evidence of viewshed impacts to both Post Oak Ridge State Park and Colorado Bend State Park.
If viewshed impacts to Palo Duro Canyon State Park were sufficient to justify rejecting lower cost,
lower habitable structure routes in Docket No. 38290, then viewshed impacts to two important
state parks in this docket cannot be dismissed merely because Link J22 falls just outside the EA’s
one-half-mile FGVZ metric.
        The PFD in Docket No. 38290 also rejected the notion that lower cost, shorter length, and
fewer habitable structures must control the routing decision. The PFD acknowledged that the
Central-South routes were “mostly commendable” for their short lengths, relatively low cost, and
low numbers of nearby habitable structures.10 But it held that those advantages were outweighed
by the strength of the community values against placing a line across Palo Duro Canyon, the
environmental costs of such a line, the engineering difficulties, and the effects on recreational
areas.11 The same type of balancing is required here. Route 894 may claim certain advantages on
cost and habitable structures, but those advantages do not outweigh its avoidable impacts on

 Colorado Bend State Park, Post Oak Ridge State Park, the Colorado River crossing area, sensitive
viewsheds, ESSS and critical habitat, and historic ranchlands.
        The similarities between Docket No. 38290 and this docket are unmistakable. In Docket
No. 38290, the concern was not that a transmission line would physically cross parkland or that it
would be in the FGVZ; it was that transmission infrastructure would “mar Palo Duro Canyon”12
and would have “visual effects on visitors to the Palo Duro Canyon state park.”13 The PFD
reasoned that efforts to mitigate the aesthetic efforts would likely be futile, finding “no reasonable
way to substantially mitigate any of these negative aesthetic effects.” 14 Here, Route 894 presents
the same problem. It places 765-kV transmission infrastructure near two important state parks and
in proximity to sensitive scenic, recreational, and river resources within those parks. Like the
routes rejected in Docket No. 38290, Route 894 performs slightly better on selected numerical
metrics (e.g., cost, length), but it performs very poorly on the qualitative factors that matter most
when iconic Texas public resources are at stake.
        The parties urging rejection of Routes CCG and 572 do not explain why the Commission’s
reasoning in Docket No. 38290 should not apply here. They do not identify a principled distinction
between avoiding unique impacts to Palo Duro Canyon State Park and avoiding similar impacts to
Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park. Nor do they explain why a more
expensive route impacting more habitable structures could be justified in Docket No. 38290 to
protect an iconic Texas resource, but Routes CCG and 572 should be categorically rejected here
because of cost and habitable structure counts. Their argument therefore proves too much. If
accepted, it would effectively convert cost and habitable structures into dispositive criteria and
erase the ALJs’ and Commission’s ability to account for unique record facts—the very flexibility
the Commission exercised in Docket No. 38290.
        The route adopted in Docket No. 38290 entirely bypassed the Palo Duro Canyon area
despite being approximately 14 miles longer and costing $17.7 million more than the route
recommended by PUC Staff.15 The route adopted was approximately eighteen-percent (18%)
longer and cost approximately ten-percent (10%) more than the PUC Staff route.16 The PFD

were justified by the route’s strong showing on community values, prudent avoidance, relative
ease of construction, effects on recreational areas, and paralleling compatible rights-of-way.17 The
Commission accepted the PFD in its Final Order.18 That same reasoning supports Routes CCG and
572 here. Route CCG best accounts for the unique facts in this record by avoiding the most serious
state park impacts associated with the central routes, using the superior J31 Colorado River
crossing, crossing the San Saba River at L4 parallel to existing transmission infrastructure,
performing well on paralleling, reducing unnecessary environmental impacts, and avoiding the
Edwards Aquifer and USFWS Karst Zone 1, as well as avoiding the historic ranchlands and
difficult terrain along Links K13 and K51. Route 572 remains a strong alternative because it
preserves many of those benefits at a cost nearly identical to Route 894.
        This case presents the same type of circumstance that made a purely numerical routing
analysis inadequate in Docket No. 38290. Route 894 may rank better on cost and habitable
structures, but it does so by imposing avoidable impacts on resources that the Commission’s
routing criteria expressly require it to consider. The Commission can and should follow the same
principle applied in Docket No. 38290: where unique public resources, scenic values,
environmental considerations, recreational impacts, and affected communities are at stake, a
higher cost or a higher habitable structure count may be justified by the complete record. As the
Hodge-Schwertner parties correctly explained, a modest cost savings does not justify a route that
performs materially worse on other statutory factors, and a large cost premium is justified by a
correspondingly large, route-wide benefit—not by a localized, crossing-level preference.19 Routes
CCG and 572 provide that route-wide benefit here.
        Route CCG’s cost exceeds Route 894 by a modest 4.38%, which is far less than the 10%
cost difference approved in Docket No. 38290, and its length exceeds Route 894 by a modest
4.04%,20 which is likewise far less than the approximate 18% difference approved in Docket No.
38290. This slightly higher estimated cost does not justify rejecting Route CCG in favor of Route
894. The relatively small cost difference must be evaluated in context. This is a project exceeding
$1.6 billion in transmission line costs alone, with cost estimates that are impacted by terrain, access

routes include the length and character of each route, including more difficult terrain. 22 That
matters because the central routes’ cost advantage may be overstated. The record and third-party
briefing confirm that difficult terrain and karst features exist along portions of the central routing
area, including Links K13 and K51. Brady Creek Intervenors describe limestone karst terrain
defined by spring-fed Brady Creek, native grassland, wooded riparian corridors, and undulating,
rugged limestone terrain.23 The Deep Creek Ranch on K13 likewise includes rugged terrain with
bluffs, caves, and wooded riparian corridors.24 These terrain conditions may increase access,
engineering, foundation, and construction complexity. Thus, the estimated cost advantage claimed
for Route 894 should not be treated as certain or controlling, particularly in light of the Applicants’
10-15% cost contingency and PUC Staff’s testimony regarding a 10% rule of thumb for comparing
route cost estimates.
         Route 572 is projected to cost a mere 0.5% more than Route 894. This difference is within
normal estimation uncertainty on a $1.68 billion project. A one-half-percent estimated cost
difference cannot reasonably justify selecting a route that performs materially worse on state park
impacts, Colorado River crossing impacts, viewshed impacts, and environmental integrity. Route
572 preserves many of the principal benefits of Route CCG, including use of the superior J31
Colorado River crossing and avoidance of the most serious central route impacts, at virtually the
same cost as Route 894.
         The habitable structure argument is also overstated. Prudent avoidance is an important
criterion, but it is not a simple “fewest habitable structures wins” test. The Commission has
selected routes that do not have the lowest number of habitable structures when other routing
considerations justified doing so.25 Here, the habitable structure differences among the Routes of
Interest are relatively modest in the context of a transmission line more than 200 miles long. Ms.
Reinecke testified that the standard deviation for habitable structures was approximately 27
structures,26 and the difference between Route CCG and Route 894 falls within one standard
deviation. Route 572 is likewise within one standard deviation. In practical terms, these routes are

           Route 894 proponents therefore ask the ALJs and Commission to treat relatively minor
differences in cost and habitable structures as dispositive even though that is inconsistent with the
law and ignores the fact that the record supports the need to weigh the unique factors in this case.
Their analysis gives insufficient weight to the central routes’ impacts on Colorado Bend State Park
and Post Oak Ridge State Park, the substantial state park viewshed evidence, the inferior Colorado
River crossings at J22 and J26, the failure to consolidate disturbance at the superior J31 crossing,
ESSS and critical habitat concerns, and the historic ranchlands along Links K13 and K51. Routes
CCG and 572 are NOT localized preferences. They provide route-long benefits.
           Route CCG remains the best route because it provides the strongest overall balance of the
Commission’s routing criteria. Route 572 remains a strong and reasonable southern alternative
because it carries forward many of those same benefits at a cost almost identical to Route 894. The
Commission should therefore reject the argument that Routes CCG and 572 must be eliminated
merely because Route 894 has a lower estimated cost and impacts fewer habitable structures.
Those factors deserve consideration, but they do not outweigh the substantial statutory and rule-
based advantages of Routes CCG and 572.

     II.     Route 894 Proponents Improperly Elevate the FGVZ Metric Over the Record’s
                                                Viewshed Evidence.
           Several parties, including the Hodge-Schwertner parties, advocate for Route 894 because
no portion of Link J22 falls within the EA’s one-half-mile foreground visual zone (“FGVZ”) for
parks and recreational areas. That argument gives the FGVZ metric more weight than it can bear.
The Hodge-Schwertner parties concede that while FGVZ is a standardized routing metric used in
the Environmental Assessment, it is “not offered as a measure of harm.”27 FGVZ is not a visibility
cutoff or a substitute for the Commission’s obligation to consider the full record regarding
community values, recreational and park areas, aesthetic values, and environmental integrity.
           As detailed previously, the PFD in Docket No. 38290 noted that Palo Duro Canyon State
Park was not within 1,000-feet of the route centerline, but this metric was not dispositive.28 The
ALJ instead focused on the view from locations several miles away from the state park.29 The route

         The Route 894 proponents use the FGVZ metric as both a sword and a shield. They use it
as a sword against Staff’s Route 487 because Links J11 and J26 fall within the one-half-mile
metric. But they then use the same metric as a shield in defense of Route 894 because Link J22 is
outside the metric (even though Link J22 comes within only 0.61 miles of Post Oak Ridge State
Park). The difference between 0.50 miles and 0.61 miles is not a meaningful distinction and has
little to do with the actual viewshed and quality of aesthetic views. A 765-kV transmission line
with massive steel structures does not become visually irrelevant simply because it is located
slightly outside a standardized one-half-mile metric.
         The FGVZ metric is not the same as a viewshed. Applicants’ Initial Post-Hearing Brief is
noteworthy for its candor on this point. Applicants’ brief confirms the limits of the Route 894
proponents’ argument. Applicants acknowledge that Route 894 uses Link J22 to cross the
Colorado River and that Link J22 comes within 0.61 miles of Post Oak Ridge State Park.
Applicants further acknowledge that this information is not captured in the routing table because
the FGVZ is measured at 0.5 miles from the park boundary.31 Applicants also acknowledge that
certain parties could and did raise the issue at the hearing and that the record contains evidence of
differing potential impacts on the viewshed from both Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak
Ridge State Park.32 Importantly, Applicants recognized that the ALJs and Commission have
significant record evidence to consider regarding visual foreground impacts on state parks in
comparing the route alternatives.33 That is the correct framework: the routing table is relevant, but
it does not end the analysis.
         Some Route 894 proponents suggest that the routing-table FGVZ is shorthand for
viewshed, but it is not. The Hodge-Schwertner Farms brief refers to FGVZ as a “standardized,
route-wide proxy”34 to suggest it is a proxy for viewshed. In the case of Route 894, it argues that
FGVZ “reflects avoidance of a concrete intrusion on a pre-existing public recreational resource.”35
To the contrary, FGVZ only reflects avoidance of an intrusion if the applicable viewshed ends at
0.5 miles. It is not a proxy for the full viewshed impacts on the state parks in this docket,

        Another party that equates viewshed with FGVZ is the J6, K41 and J33 Landowner Group
which argues, “Route 894 protects the aesthetics of the area by utilizing the J22 Colorado River
crossing, which is out of the one-half mile distance, referred to as viewshed in the environmental

Applicants specifically acknowledge this reality, some intervenors do not.
        The Commission’s routing criteria are not limited to what appears in a routing table. The
FGVZ metric does not measure, and is not intended to measure, all viewshed impacts, all aesthetic
impacts, or all community value impacts. A viewshed is the actual area from which the
transmission line may be visible, depending on topography, vegetation, tower height, ridgelines,
viewer location, and other site-specific conditions. The evidence in the record confirms that a
proper viewshed analysis must look beyond a one-half-mile line on a table. A route may fall
outside the one-half-mile FGVZ and still materially affect the scenic quality, visitor experience,
viewshed, and recreational value of a state park. That is particularly true here, where the record
includes photographs of the relevant viewsheds,38 testimony regarding scenic quality as part of the
state park experience,39 and a Texas State Parks viewshed analysis addressing the visibility of
transmission facilities within five miles of scenic viewpoints valued for their natural qualities.40
        The Yates Keith Alliance argument that a transmission line outside a park or recreational
area will not prevent people from using that park41 misses the point. The issue is not merely
whether visitors can physically enter Colorado Bend State Park or Post Oak Ridge State Park after
the line is built. The issue is whether the line will materially degrade the scenic, recreational, and
aesthetic experience those parks exist to provide. Visitors do not go to Colorado Bend State Park
or Post Oak Ridge State Park simply to stand on park property. The 56,000 annual visitors to
Colorado Bend State Park42 and the estimated 70,000 annual visitors to Post Oak Ridge State
Park43 go to experience the Hill Country landscape, river corridors, waterfalls, overlooks, trails,

J22 is 0.50 miles or 0.61 miles from a park boundary. The proper question is whether the route
best moderates impacts on affected communities and landowners while properly accounting for
community values, recreational and park areas, aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and the
full record evidence. On that record, Routes CCG and 572 are superior to Route 894 because they
avoid the most serious state park viewshed concerns associated with the central routes, and better

                                      VII.     CONCLUSION
       The proponents of Route 894 ask the ALJs and Commission to reduce a record developed
by hundreds of intervenors in a 5-day Hearing on the Merits to a narrow comparison of selected
metrics: cost and habitable structures. The Commission's routing rules require more, including
consideration ofthe unique circumstances of the docket.
       As noted above, the entire purpose of the instant process is to identify the route that best
meets all of the routing criteria to minimize the harm caused by the transmission lines. The design
of Route CCG minimizes the harm caused by Route 894 to the Colorado State Park, the Post Oak
Ridge State Park, the Colorado River, the San Saba River, Golden-Cheek Warbler habitat, the
oldest continuously operated ranches on the record, the Edwards Aquifer and USFWS Karst Zone
1, as well as maximizing paralleling and avoiding the difficult terrain on Segments K13 and K51.
The determinative question in this case is whether these significant and numerous benefits are
worth an increase in cost and length of less than 5% and a slight (within one standard deviation)
increase in habitable structures.
       Here, the ALJs and Commission have "significant record evidence" to consider regarding
visual impacts on state parks in comparing the route alternatives. That evidence should not be
displaced by the EA's FGVZ metric. What the Commission decided in Docket No. 38290 is
instructive. Protecting the viewshed at a state park supports community values, parks and
recreational areas, and aesthetic concerns.
       Isolated GCW testimony focused on one link, trinomial arguments that elevate bureaucracy
over historic significance, or notice arguments inconsistent with Commission precedent, should be
rejected and not given any weight in determining which route best meets all of the routing criteria.
       Based on a careful and thoughtful weighing of all factors the law requires the ALJs and the
Commission to consider, Route CCG is the best meets route. Route CCG avoids the most serious
state park impacts associated with the central routes, uses the superior J31 Colorado River
crossing, crosses the San Saba River at L4 parallel to existing transmission infrastructure, performs
better than Route 894 on paralleling, reduces unnecessary environmental impacts, and avoids the
historic ranchlands and difficult terrain along Links K13 and K51. If the ALJs and Commission
prefer a route with a cost almost identical to Route 894 that captures many of Route CCG' s
benefits, including avoidance of the most serious state park impacts and use of the J31 Colorado
River crossing, Route 572 is the best alternative. The limited cost and habitable structure
